metadata.title: IR band map for CO2 hydrogenation
metadata.description: Approximate band positions for surface and gas-phase species in CO₂ hydrogenation. Exact positions depend on support, coverage, and reaction conditions. The asterisk (*) denotes a surface-bound species.

bands.description: Gas CO₂ antisymmetric stretch (ν₃) — R-branch (ΔJ = +1) at ~2360 cm⁻¹. Higher-frequency rotational envelope; pair-mate of the P-branch at ~2335. Q-branch forbidden (Σ→Σ transition), leaving a characteristic gap at the band origin (~2349). Saturates at high pressure.

Gas CO₂ antisymmetric stretch (ν₃) — P-branch (ΔJ = −1) at ~2335 cm⁻¹. Lower-frequency rotational envelope; pair-mate of the R-branch at ~2360. Q-branch forbidden (Σ→Σ transition); band origin at ~2349 cm⁻¹. Saturates at high pressure.

Gas CO₂ bending fundamental (ν₂) — R-branch (ΔJ = +1) at ~700 cm⁻¹. Higher-frequency rotational envelope; pair-mate of the P-branch at ~660. Q-branch is allowed (Σ→Π transition) and appears as a sharp spike at ~667 between P and R envelopes.

Gas CO₂ bending fundamental (ν₂) — Q-branch (ΔJ = 0) at ~667 cm⁻¹. Sharp, intense spike between P and R envelopes; allowed because ν₂ is a Σ→Π (perpendicular) transition. Saturates very quickly at modest pCO₂.

Gas CO₂ bending fundamental (ν₂) — P-branch (ΔJ = −1) at ~660 cm⁻¹. Lower-frequency rotational envelope; pair-mate of the R-branch at ~700. Atmospheric CO₂ in the beam path contributes to this region; routinely seen even with good purging.
Gas CO₂ combination band at ~3730 cm⁻¹; (ν₁ + ν₃) R-branch — upper Fermi-resonance component, R-side. Useful for high-pressure quantification when the ν_as fundamental saturates.

based_on.label: ν₁ sym stretch CO₂ (IR-inactive, not in dataset)

bands.description: Gas CO₂ combination band at ~3699 cm⁻¹; (ν₁ + ν₃) P-branch — upper Fermi-resonance component, P-side. P/R-branch separation ~30 cm⁻¹; pair-mate of the R-branch at ~3730.

based_on.label: ν₁ sym stretch CO₂ (IR-inactive, not in dataset)

bands.description: Gas CO₂ combination band at ~3627 cm⁻¹; (2ν₂ + ν₃) R-branch — lower Fermi-resonance component, R-side. Separation between Fermi pair (3730 vs 3627) ~107 cm⁻¹ is fixed.
Gas CO₂ combination band at ~3597 cm⁻¹; (2ν₂ + ν₃) P-branch — lower Fermi-resonance component, P-side. P/R-branch separation ~30 cm⁻¹; pair-mate of the R-branch at ~3627.

Gas CO₂ combination band at ~2077 cm⁻¹; (11101 ← 00001) Q-branch — the most intense combination band in the 2200-1900 cm⁻¹ region. Falls in the typical metal-carbonyl stretching range and has been repeatedly misassigned in DRIFTS studies of Cu-based methanol synthesis catalysts as ν(CO) on Cu(0)/Cu(111)/low-index Cu planes. Particularly pronounced in long-path-length cells (e.g. Praying Mantis HTRC) and amplified at higher CO₂ pressures and temperatures. Always check for this band before assigning a 2077 cm⁻¹ feature to surface CO.

Gas-phase CO stretch (ν) — R-branch (ΔJ = +1) at ~2170 cm⁻¹. Higher-frequency rotational envelope; pair-mate of the P-branch at ~2115. Q-branch forbidden for diatomic CO (Σ→Σ transition), leaving a characteristic gap at ~2143 cm⁻¹ between R and P branches.

Gas-phase CO stretch (ν) — P-branch (ΔJ = −1) at ~2115 cm⁻¹. Lower-frequency rotational envelope; pair-mate of the R-branch at ~2170. P/R splitting ~55 cm⁻¹ at room temperature; envelope broadens and shifts intensity to higher-J lines as temperature increases (Maxwell–Boltzmann redistribution).
Gas methane antisymmetric C-H stretch (ν₃, T₂ mode); sharp Q-branch at ~3019 cm⁻¹ with rotational P/R structure.
Gas methane antisymmetric bending (ν₄, T₂ mode) at ~1306 cm⁻¹.
Gas methane combination band at ~4220 cm⁻¹; useful for high-pressure quantification when ν_as saturates. Often outside standard DRIFTS window.
Physisorbed methane (CH₄*) on the catalyst surface; red-shifted from gas-phase by 10-30 cm⁻¹. Asterisk denotes surface adsorption.

Linear (atop) CO bonded to a single metal atom. Most common adsorption mode on Cu, Pt, Pd, Rh, Ni, and Co surfaces. Frequency depends on metal identity, oxidation state, coordination environment, and surface coverage due to π-backdonation and dipole coupling. Typical values: Cu⁰ ~2080–2100, Pt ~2070, Rh ~2050 cm⁻¹. Electron-poor or partially oxidized sites shift to higher frequency. Asterisk denotes surface adsorption.

Bridging CO coordinated between two metal atoms. Lower frequency than linear CO due to increased metal→CO π-backdonation from multiple metal centers. Common on Pt, Pd, Rh, Ni, and Co surfaces; less common on Cu and typically observed only at high coverage or defect sites. Often associated with step and edge sites.

Three-fold hollow CO coordinated to three metal atoms. Common on close-packed Pt, Pd, Rh, and Ni surfaces at moderate-to-high CO coverage. Rare on Cu surfaces. Stronger multi-center π-backdonation shifts ν(CO) to lower frequency than bridge or linear adsorption.

Four-fold hollow CO coordinated to four metal atoms. Rare adsorption geometry reported mainly on Ni(100), Co, and related surfaces. Exhibits the lowest ν(CO) frequencies among metal–CO adsorption modes due to strong multi-center π-backdonation.

Linear CO adsorbed on Lewis-acidic metal cation sites of oxide supports, zeolites, or isolated metal centers. Reduced metal→CO π-backdonation shifts ν(CO) to higher frequency than on metallic surfaces. Typical values: Cu⁺ ~2100–2130, Cu²⁺ ~2150–2180, Ce³⁺ ~2130, Ce⁴⁺ ~2160, Ti⁴⁺ ~2190, Zn²⁺ ~2200, and Al³⁺/Mg²⁺ ~2210 cm⁻¹. Widely used as a probe of Lewis acidity and oxidation state.

Isocarbonyl species with CO coordinated through oxygen rather than carbon (M–OC). Rare adsorption mode observed on highly oxidized surfaces, strongly electrophilic cations, and certain zeolite environments. Typically exhibits higher ν(CO) frequency than conventional C-bound carbonyls.

Antisymmetric ν(CO) component of geminal dicarbonyl species with two linear CO ligands bound to a single isolated cationic metal center, typically Rh⁺, Ir⁺, Ru⁺, or Cu⁺. The symmetric/asymmetric pair is diagnostic of atomically dispersed cationic sites. Typical splitting: ~50–60 cm⁻¹.

Symmetric ν(CO) component of geminal dicarbonyl species with two linear CO ligands bound to a single isolated cationic metal center. Appears together with the antisymmetric band and is characteristic of isolated cationic adsorption sites.

Surface formyl C=O stretch (HCO*); mechanistic intermediate from CO + H. Often observed transiently. Distinguishes the CO-H pathway from formate-mediated routes. Asterisk denotes surface intermediate.
Formyl C-H stretch (HCO*); lower than formate ν(CH) at ~2870-2900 and weaker. Diagnostic when paired with C=O at ~1750.
Adsorbed formaldehyde C=O stretch (H₂CO*); reduction product of formyl. Key methanol precursor in some mechanisms.
Adsorbed formaldehyde CH₂ antisymmetric stretch (H₂CO*).
Adsorbed formaldehyde CH₂ symmetric stretch (H₂CO*).
Adsorbed formaldehyde CH₂ scissoring (H₂CO*); overlaps monodentate carbonate ν_as.
Generic surface acyl/aldehyde C=O stretch (R-C=O*); broad assignment used when species cannot be specifically identified. Distinguishes from formate by absence of ν(CH) at ~2870.
Hydroxymethyl O-H stretch (H₂COH*); late methanol precursor. Often masked by surface OH.
Hydroxymethyl CH₂ stretch (H₂COH*); overlaps methoxy and methanol.
Hydroxymethyl C-O stretch (H₂COH*); overlaps methoxy ν(C-O) at ~1050-1100.
Bidentate carbonate antisymmetric stretch (b-CO₃²⁻*); large splitting (Δν ~300 cm⁻¹). Asterisk denotes surface adsorption.
Bidentate carbonate symmetric stretch (b-CO₃²⁻*).
Bidentate carbonate antisymmetric stretch first overtone (b-CO₃²⁻*); rare but reported.
Monodentate carbonate antisymmetric stretch (m-CO₃²⁻*); small splitting (Δν ~100 cm⁻¹). Asterisk denotes surface adsorption.
Monodentate carbonate symmetric stretch (m-CO₃²⁻*).
Monodentate carbonate antisymmetric stretch first overtone (m-CO₃²⁻*); rare but reported.
Carbonate OCO bending (CO₃²⁻*).
Bicarbonate antisymmetric OCO stretch (HCO₃⁻*). Asterisk denotes surface adsorption.
Bicarbonate symmetric OCO stretch (HCO₃⁻*).
Bicarbonate COH bending (HCO₃⁻*); distinguishing feature vs. carbonate.
Formate C-H stretch (HCOO*); key HCOO* marker. Asterisk denotes surface adsorption.
Formate antisymmetric OCO stretch (HCOO*); key HCOO* marker.
Formate symmetric OCO stretch (HCOO*).
Formate C-H bending (HCOO*); overlaps ν_s(OCO).
Formate combination band (HCOO*): bending + antisymmetric stretch; diagnostic for HCOO*.
Formate higher combination band (HCOO*); sometimes assigned as 2ν(C=O) overtone in older literature.
Methoxy CH₃ antisymmetric stretch (CH₃O*). Asterisk denotes surface adsorption.
Methoxy CH₃ symmetric stretch (CH₃O*).
Methoxy CH₃ deformation (CH₃O*).
Methoxy C-O stretch (CH₃O*).
Methanol O-H stretch (MeOH*/MeOH(g)); often obscured by adsorbed water.
Methanol C-H stretches (MeOH*/MeOH(g)).
Methanol C-O stretch (MeOH*/MeOH(g)).
Sharp band; isolated terminal hydroxyls on metal-oxide supports. Asterisk denotes surface species.
Broader band; bridged or hydrogen-bonded hydroxyls. Asterisk denotes surface species.
Very broad O-H stretch of adsorbed/condensed water (H₂O*). Asterisk denotes surface adsorption.
Water bending mode (H₂O*); overlaps formate ν_as.
Cu hydride (Cu-H*); weak, often hidden under carbonate/methoxy bands. Asterisk denotes surface species.
ZnO hydride (Zn-H*); classic marker for heterolytic H₂ dissociation on Cu/ZnO. Asterisk denotes surface species.
OH partner of heterolytic H₂ splitting on ZnO; rises in tandem with Zn-H*.
Cerium hydride (Ce-H*) on reduced CeO₂.
Mo hydride (Mo-H*) on reduced MoOₓ.
Gallium hydride (Ga-H*) on Ga₂O₃-based catalysts; activity marker for heterolytic H₂ dissociation.
Rhodium hydride (Rh-H*) on supported Rh catalysts; observed on Rh single-atom and atomically-dispersed sites. Often paired with gem-dicarbonyl signatures for Rh⁺ identification.
Lithium hydride (Li-H*) on LiH-containing or Li-doped systems. Rare in CO₂ hydrogenation literature; more common in nitrogen activation (LiH/Mn4N).
Support lattice modes (ZnO, CeO₂, TiO₂, Al₂O₃); window-dependent cutoff.
Support lattice mode first overtone; can be mistaken for surface species.
